\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{こい} (koi)}{こい (koi)}]{\ja{こい} (koi) — a carp}

\label{lesson:JA-C65-koi}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a sardine, then the Japanese for a flavour.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{こい}}
\textbf{\ja{こい}} — \emph{koi} — \textquotedblleft{}a carp\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{こい}} (\emph{koi}) is a native Japanese word, inherited rather than borrowed from Chinese, and its older origin is not settled. Its kanji was attached to it later as a kun'yomi, a native reading given to a Chinese character (JMdict, KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{せみ}}
\textbf{\ja{せみ}} — \emph{semi} — \textquotedblleft{}a cicada\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{せみ}} (\emph{semi}) is the kun'yomi of the character for the cicada and is counted a native word; a link with the Chinese word for the cicada has been suggested, and its origin is not settled (KANJIDIC2).
\end{cousinweb}

\section[\texorpdfstring{\ja{ごぼう} (gobou)}{ごぼう (gobou)}]{\ja{ごぼう} (gobou) — burdock root}

\label{lesson:JA-C65-gobou}



\begin{quote}
Before the new one: say the Japanese for a dragonfly, then the Japanese for a potato.
\end{quote}

\subsection*{You'll want to know: \ja{ごぼう}}
\textbf{\ja{ごぼう}} — \emph{gobou} — \textquotedblleft{}burdock root\textquotedblright{}.

\begin{cousinweb}
\textbf{\ja{ごぼう}} (\emph{gobou}) is Sino-Japanese (kango): two Chinese characters read with their on'yomi, readings borrowed from Chinese. They are \emph{go}, \textquotedblleft{}ox, cow\textquotedblright{} (Middle Chinese \emph{ngjuw}) and \emph{bō}, \textquotedblleft{}burdock\textquotedblright{} (\emph{pangX}) (Unihan, KANJIDIC2; Middle Chinese in Baxter's transcription). JMdict marks it as usually written in kana.
\end{cousinweb}
